Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
There is something wrong with me as a person
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The Negative Appraisals node is internally inconsistent for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. 'Intrinsic Fault' fits a child abuse formulation, but 'Violated Values' implies the patient believes she herself committed morally troubling actions, which is hard to reconcile with being a child victim unless there is additional unreported perpetration or compliance behavior. 'Physical Vulnerability' as permanent bodily damage is also a distinct injury-based appraisal that is not supported elsewhere in the profile. Taken together, these three appraisals do not form a coherent single appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: 'Being in Nature' is difficult to reconcile with the trauma type of repeated physical abuse by a caregiver unless the abuse specifically occurred in a natural/outdoor setting. The rest of the profile points to interpersonal danger, shame, and hypervigilance rather than context-specific outdoor reminders, so this trigger looks trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, the selected negative appraisals are mostly coherent when they center on shame, defectiveness, and self-blame (e.g., intrinsic fault, defective self). However, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies perpetration or morally troubling behavior by the patient, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there is additional context not represented elsewhere. Within the node, it pulls in a different direction from the other appraisals, which depict the patient as harmed/defective rather than as having committed value-violating actions.

vignette:
Amara, a 43-year-old IT support specialist living in a Midwestern suburb, carries the aftermath of a childhood that unfolded in a small, rural house with a locked tool shed behind it. Her mother, her primary caregiver, would order her into that shed, bolt the door from the outside, and beat her with a garden hose in the dim, earthy light that filtered through the cracks in the wooden walls. The smell of damp soil and rusted metal, the sound of her own breath inside the confined space, the helplessness of being trapped—those sensations lodged themselves in her body long before she had words for them. Now, decades later, Amara believes that there must have been something inherently wrong with her that made her mother do those things. She has never shaken the conviction that she is fundamentally defective, that the abuse happened because of the sort of person she is—weak, deserving of punishment, somehow broken at the core.

That self-appraisal keeps her body in a permanent state of readiness. Her muscles stay taut, her shoulders hunched, her jaw clenched; she feels constantly tense, as if danger could appear from any direction at any moment. At work, in the open-plan IT office, she has trouble concentrating on help-desk tickets because her attention is split between the computer screen and scanning for sudden movements or raised voices. Sometimes she startles violently when a coworker taps her shoulder, her heart hammering even after she realizes the threat is imagined. These false alarms—reacting as if she is in danger when nothing is actually wrong—only deepen her belief that she is broken. Each racing heartbeat and trembling hand feels like proof that something is wrong with her, that her body is betraying her because she is, at bottom, defective. She wonders why she cannot just be normal, and that question loops back into more tension, more scanning.

Amara avoids what she can. She never talks about the abuse; even a casual mention of childhood by a colleague makes her chest tighten and her mind go blank, and she has learned to steer conversations away from any personal history. She also avoids natural settings—parks, wooded trails, even the small courtyard outside her office building. The sight of trees and open grass pulls her back to that shed’s doorway, to the moment of being pushed inside. And locked spaces terrify her. She refuses to use the supply closet at work, and when a server-room door clicked shut behind her last month, her breath stopped and she had to press her palms against the wall until someone opened it. The trigger—the locked room—does not just happen to her; it is made more potent by her constant threat monitoring. Because she is always on edge, the click of a lock or the sight of a forest path does not merely remind her of the past; it feels like an immediate crisis, a confirmation that danger is real and present. And at the same time, her negative appraisals amplify the trigger: being in a locked room reinforces her belief that she is the kind of person who attracts harm, that the environment itself is punishing her for being who she is.

Over the months, this cycle has tightened. She has begun to take longer routes to avoid passing the office courtyard. She has stopped volunteering for any task that might require her to retrieve equipment from the storage closet. Her husband, Jerome, has noticed that she flinches when he closes the bedroom door at night, and he has asked her repeatedly what is wrong—but she cannot bring herself to talk about it. The marital strain is a quiet, accumulating weight. What finally brought Amara to therapy was a panic attack last week in a conference room. The door had a faulty latch, and when it clicked shut during a meeting, she felt her throat close, her vision tunnel, and she fled without explanation, leaving her team staring. She sat in the bathroom for twenty minutes, trembling, certain she was falling apart. Now she sits in a therapist’s office, afraid that if she tells the story aloud she will be confirming once and for all that she is defective—but also desperate to stop living inside her own alarm system.
